newsitem.title: USA: Fund strategies for college savings.
newsitem.headline: Fund strategies for college savings.

text.p: Ask Americans about their financial goals and they will talk about buying a home, saving enough for a secure and comfortable retirement and putting their children through college.

Most of us rely on mortgages to meet the first goal, making monthly payments to achieve our goal of home ownership. As for retirement, we have pensions, retirement savings accounts such as IRAs and 40l(k)s, and -- who knows? -- we might even get something back from Social Security.

That leaves college. By now, you've probably heard the horrifying numbers: A year's worth of tuition, room and board at a public college costs an average of around $11,000, and the tab is closer to $22,000 at private schools. That's not as bad as it sounds: You might be able to pay some of that cost from your income, or rely on financial aid to ease the burden. You almost certainly can land some hefty, low-cost loans through government programmes such as the Federal Direct Student Loan Programme (800-524-9100).

Still, it would be nice if you could pay for some of those costs out of savings, reducing the strain during and after a child's college years. The best way to build up those savings may be to choose a mutual fund or two that will provide as much growth as possible between now and the time you receive your children's tuition bills.

Which funds? If a child is five or more years from college, go for growth with funds that invest at least some of their assets in the stock market. A good choice: T. Rowe Price Spectrum Growth (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum investment; no load), which invests in a combination of other growth-oriented T. Rowe Price stock funds. As such, it offers investors exposure to various equity sectors, such as small, medium-sized, and large company stocks, as well as international stocks.

Closer to college, you'll want to avoid severe fluctuations in the value of your savings. Thus, a gradual shift of some money to income-oriented funds will make sense. Spectrum Growth's sister fund, Spectrum Income (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no load), invests in several T. Rowe Price bond funds including High Yield Fund; GNMA Fund and International Bond. (You can avoid the Spectrum Funds' minimum $2,500 initial investment by pledging to invest $50 each month through an automatic investment plan.)

Some financial advisers recommend custodial accounts for college savings. Such accounts are established under the Uniform Gifts/Transfers to Minors Act, and are commonly called UGMA or UTMA accounts. When your child is under age 14, the first $650 of income from the account is exempt from taxes; the next $650 is taxed at the child's presumably low rate (typically 15 percent). Income above $1,300 is taxed at your highest marginal rate. Once the child turns 14, all of the income is taxed at the child's rate--an even better deal.
By contrast, if you hold the child's college investments in your name, all the profits are taxed at your rate -- which will likely be much higher than the child's tax bracket.

But there are reasons to forgo that tax break. For starters, your child at age 18 or 21 will be able to spend the money as he or she likes -- and he or she might decide that for the moment a new car matters more than college.

Moreover, your custodial account might make it harder to get financial aid. That's because schools expect students to spend as much as 35 percent of their savings on tuition costs, while parents are only expected to spend 5.6 percent. A large amount in a child's name might reduce his or her chances for financial aid.

Finally, the tax breaks you'll earn in a custodial account generally are relatively modest in terms of dollar amounts; thus, they often aren't worth the risk that your child might misspend the money or lose out on financial aid.

For now, you can put off the decision about whether to use a custodial account for college savings. But don't put off saving itself: The sooner you get started, the sooner your investments can start working to help you put your child through college.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
